nodes.label: Term 2 · Unit 3 — Probability
nodes.description: Second-term probability unit: probability of an event P(A) = n(A)/n(S), operations on events (intersection, union, mutually exclusive events, Venn diagrams), the complementary event, and the difference between two events.

nodes.label: Probability of an event: P(A) = n(A)/n(S)
nodes.description: Write the sample space S of a random experiment; for an event A ⊂ S compute P(A) = n(A)/n(S); recognize the impossible event (P = 0), the certain event (P = 1), and place probabilities on the scale from 0 to 1 written as fractions or percentages.

nodes.label: Intersection of two events and mutually exclusive events
nodes.description: For events A, B of a sample space S, form A ∩ B — the event that A and B occur together — using Venn diagrams; compute P(A ∩ B) = n(A ∩ B)/n(S); recognize mutually exclusive events, where A ∩ B = φ and P(A ∩ B) = 0.

nodes.label: Union of two events and the addition rule
nodes.description: Form A ∪ B — the occurrence of A or B or both (at least one event) — and compute its probability by counting or by the rule P(A ∪ B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A ∩ B); for mutually exclusive events P(A ∪ B) = P(A) + P(B).

nodes.label: The complementary event
nodes.description: For A ⊂ S, the complementary event A′ satisfies A ∪ A′ = S and A ∩ A′ = φ (the event and its complement are mutually exclusive); use P(A) + P(A′) = 1, i.e. P(A′) = 1 − P(A).

nodes.label: The difference between two events
nodes.description: A − B is the event that A occurs and B does not occur (the occurrence of A only); note that (A − B) ∪ (A ∩ B) = A; apply it with Venn diagrams to 'only one' and 'exactly one' problems.

questions.stem: A regular die is rolled once and the upper face is observed. The probability of getting a number less than 7 equals …
solution: Write the sample space: $S = \{1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6\}$, so $n(S) = 6$.
The event of getting a number less than 7 is $\{1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6\} = S$ itself, so its number of elements $= 6$.
$P(\text{number} < 7) = \dfrac{6}{6} = 1$ — every face of the die is less than 7, so it is a certain event and its probability is $1$.
questions.source_note: Original question; certain event from the dice Think-and-Discuss (number less than 9 → less than 7), p.30

questions.stem: A regular die is rolled once. The probability of getting the number 8 equals …
solution: The sample space is $S = \{1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6\}$ and $n(S) = 6$.
The event of getting 8 has no elements in $S$ (the die has no face 8), so it is the impossible event: its set is $\phi$ and $n(\phi) = 0$.
$P(\text{getting } 8) = \dfrac{0}{6} = 0$.
questions.source_note: Original question; impossible event from the dice Think-and-Discuss (having 7 → having 8), p.30

questions.stem: A box contains 6 white balls and 4 red balls. If a ball is drawn randomly, calculate the probability that the drawn ball is red.
solution: The box contains $6 + 4 = 10$ identical balls, all equally likely to be drawn, so $n(S) = 10$.
The event of drawing a red ball has $n(A) = 4$ elements.
$P(\text{red}) = \dfrac{n(A)}{n(S)} = \dfrac{4}{10} = \dfrac{2}{5} = 0.4$.
questions.source_note: Original variant of Drill 1 (3 white + 4 red → 6 white + 4 red), p.30

questions.stem: A spinner is divided into 10 equal sectors: 4 green, 3 yellow, 2 blue and 1 red. The probability that the indicator stops on a yellow sector equals …
solution: The 10 sectors are equal, so all outcomes are equally likely and $n(S) = 10$.
The yellow sectors are $3$, so $n(\text{yellow}) = 3$.
$P(\text{yellow}) = \dfrac{n(\text{yellow})}{n(S)} = \dfrac{3}{10}$.
questions.source_note: Original variant of Drill 2 (8-sector spinner → 10 sectors, new colors), p.31

questions.stem: A set of identical cards numbered from 1 to 8 is mixed well and a card is drawn randomly. The probability that the drawn card has a prime number equals …
solution: The sample space is $S = \{1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8\}$, so $n(S) = 8$.
The event of drawing a prime number is $B = \{2, 3, 5, 7\}$, so $n(B) = 4$ (remember: 1 is not prime).
$P(B) = \dfrac{n(B)}{n(S)} = \dfrac{4}{8} = \dfrac{1}{2}$.
questions.source_note: Original single-event question from the cards 1–8 example (event B: prime), p.31

questions.stem: If the probability of an event is $P(A) = \dfrac{3}{4}$, write $P(A)$ as a percentage. (Answer in %.)
solution: Probability can be written as a fraction or as a percentage.
So $P(A) = 75\%$ — on the probability scale this is 'more likely' (between $\frac{1}{2}$ and the certain event 1).
questions.source_note: Original question; fraction-percentage probability scale box, p.30

questions.stem: Which of the following values CANNOT be the probability of an event?
solution: For any event $A \subset S$: $0 \le n(A) \le n(S)$, so $P(A) = \dfrac{n(A)}{n(S)}$ is always between 0 and 1.
$P = 0$ is the impossible event and $P = 1$ is the certain event; $0.25 = \frac{1}{4}$ lies between them on the scale.
$1.2 > 1$, so it cannot be the probability of any event.
questions.source_note: Original question; probability scale 0 → 1 (impossible … certain), p.30

questions.stem: Identical cards numbered from 1 to 12 are mixed well and one card is drawn randomly. Find the probability that the drawn card has a number divisible by 4.
solution: The sample space is $S = \{1, 2, 3, \dots, 12\}$, so $n(S) = 12$.
The event of a number divisible by 4 is $A = \{4, 8, 12\}$, so $n(A) = 3$.
questions.source_note: Original variant of the cards example (1–8, divisible by 4 → 1–12), p.31

questions.stem: If A and B are two events from a sample space S, then $A \cap B$ means …

choices.text: the occurrence of the two events A and B together
the occurrence of at least one of the two events

solution: Events are subsets of the sample space S, so operations on events are like operations on sets.
The intersection $A \cap B$ means the events A and B occur together — the outcome of the experiment belongs to both sets.
The occurrence of at least one event is the union $A \cup B$, and the occurrence of A only is the difference $A - B$.
questions.source_note: Original question; definition of intersection of two events, p.31

questions.stem: It is said that A and B are two mutually exclusive events if …
solution: A and B are mutually exclusive events if $A \cap B = \phi$: the two events cannot occur at the same time.
In the Venn diagram they appear as two separate (distant) sets, and $P(A \cap B) = \dfrac{0}{n(S)} = 0$.
questions.source_note: Original question; mutually exclusive events definition box, p.32

questions.stem: Identical cards numbered from 1 to 10 are mixed well and a card is drawn randomly. Event A: the card has an even number; event B: the card has a prime number. The probability that A and B occur together equals …
solution: Occurring together means $A \cap B = \{2\}$ — the only even prime — so $n(A \cap B) = 1$.
$P(A \cap B) = \dfrac{n(A \cap B)}{n(S)} = \dfrac{1}{10}$.
questions.source_note: Original variant of the cards 1–8 intersection example (→ cards 1–10, even ∩ prime), p.31

questions.stem: A regular die is rolled once. Event A: getting an even number; event B: getting a number greater than 3. Find $n(A \cap B)$, the number of elements of the event that A and B occur together.
solution: $A \cap B = \{4, 6\}$ — the outcomes that are even AND greater than 3.
So $n(A \cap B) = 2$ (and $P(A \cap B) = \frac{2}{6} = \frac{1}{3}$).
questions.source_note: Original variant of the dice drill (even/odd/prime-even events → even ∩ greater than 3), p.32

questions.stem: A regular die is rolled once. Event A: getting an even number; event B: getting an odd number. The probability of the occurrence of A and B together equals …
solution: A number cannot be even and odd at the same time, so $A \cap B = \phi$ and $n(A \cap B) = 0$: A and B are mutually exclusive events.
$P(A \cap B) = \dfrac{0}{6} = 0$.
questions.source_note: Original question; dice drill events A (even) and B (odd) are mutually exclusive, p.32

questions.stem: Identical cards numbered from 1 to 12 are mixed well and a card is drawn randomly. Event A: the number is divisible by 3; event B: the number is divisible by 4. Then $P(A \cap B)$ equals …
solution: $A \cap B = \{12\}$ — the only number from 1 to 12 divisible by both 3 and 4 — so $n(A \cap B) = 1$.
$P(A \cap B) = \dfrac{1}{12}$.
questions.source_note: Original question; intersection with divisibility events on cards 1–12, extends p.31 example

questions.stem: A regular die is rolled once. Which pair of events is MUTUALLY EXCLUSIVE?

choices.text: getting an even number ; getting an odd number
getting an even number ; getting a prime number
getting an odd number ; getting a prime number
getting a number greater than 2 ; getting a number less than 5

solution: Two events are mutually exclusive when their intersection is $\phi$ — they cannot occur at the same time.
Even $\{2,4,6\}$ and odd $\{1,3,5\}$: intersection $= \phi$ ✓ mutually exclusive.

Even $\{2,4,6\}$ and prime $\{2,3,5\}$ share $\{2\}$; odd $\{1,3,5\}$ and prime $\{2,3,5\}$ share $\{3,5\}$; greater than 2 $\{3,4,5,6\}$ and less than 5 $\{1,2,3,4\}$ share $\{3,4\}$ — none of these are mutually exclusive.
questions.source_note: Original question; identifying mutually exclusive pairs on the die, p.32

questions.stem: A and B are two events of a sample space S of a random experiment where $n(S) = 20$ and $n(A \cap B) = 5$. Find the probability of the occurrence of the two events together.
solution: The probability of the occurrence of A and B together is $P(A \cap B) = \dfrac{n(A \cap B)}{n(S)}$.
Substitute: $P(A \cap B) = \dfrac{5}{20} = \dfrac{1}{4} = 0.25$.
questions.source_note: Original question; applying P(A ∩ B) = n(A ∩ B)/n(S) directly, p.32

questions.stem: If A and B are two events from a sample space S, then $A \cup B$ means the occurrence of …

choices.text: at least one of the two events (A or B or both)

solution: The union $A \cup B$ means the occurrence of the two events A or B or both.
In other words: the occurrence of at least one of the two events.
The occurrence of the two events together is the intersection $A \cap B$.
questions.source_note: Original question; definition of union of two events, p.32

questions.stem: For any two events A and B of a sample space S, $P(A \cup B)$ equals …
solution: Adding $P(A) + P(B)$ counts the elements of $A \cap B$ twice, so we subtract them once.
$P(A \cup B) = P(A) + P(B) - P(A \cap B)$.
Only when A and B are mutually exclusive ($A \cap B = \phi$, $P(A \cap B) = 0$) does this become $P(A \cup B) = P(A) + P(B)$.
questions.source_note: Original question; the rule discovered in Example 1 part C, pp.33-34

questions.stem: A and B are two events in the sample space of a random experiment where $P(A) = 0.3$, $P(B) = 0.4$ and $P(A \cap B) = 0.2$. Find $P(A \cup B)$.
solution: $P(A \cup B) = P(A) + P(B) - P(A \cap B)$.
Substitute: $P(A \cup B) = 0.3 + 0.4 - 0.2$.
questions.source_note: Original variant of Drill 1-A (0.2, 0.6, 0.3 → 0.3, 0.4, 0.2), p.34

questions.stem: A and B are two MUTUALLY EXCLUSIVE events where $P(A) = 0.35$ and $P(B) = 0.25$. Find $P(A \cup B)$.
solution: A and B are mutually exclusive, so $A \cap B = \phi$ and $P(A \cap B) = 0$.
$P(A \cup B) = P(A) + P(B) - P(A \cap B) = P(A) + P(B)$.
questions.source_note: Original question; union rule for mutually exclusive events, p.34

questions.stem: Identical cards numbered from 1 to 10 are mixed well and a card is drawn randomly. Event A: the number is even; event B: the number is divisible by 3. The probability of the occurrence of A or B equals …
solution: Occurrence of A or B means $A \cup B = \{2, 3, 4, 6, 8, 9, 10\}$, so $n(A \cup B) = 7$.
$P(A \cup B) = \dfrac{n(A \cup B)}{n(S)} = \dfrac{7}{10}$.
Check by the rule: $P(A) + P(B) - P(A \cap B) = \dfrac{5}{10} + \dfrac{3}{10} - \dfrac{1}{10} = \dfrac{7}{10}$ ✓ (since $A \cap B = \{6\}$).
questions.source_note: Original variant of Example 1 (9 cards, even ∪ divisible by 3 → 10 cards), p.33

questions.stem: A and B are two events in the sample space of a random experiment where $P(A) = 0.5$, $P(B) = 0.6$ and $P(A \cup B) = 0.8$. Find $P(A \cap B)$.
solution: From the rule $P(A \cup B) = P(A) + P(B) - P(A \cap B)$, we get $P(A \cap B) = P(A) + P(B) - P(A \cup B)$.
Substitute: $P(A \cap B) = 0.5 + 0.6 - 0.8$.
questions.source_note: Original variant of Drill 1-B (find the missing probability from the union rule), p.34

questions.stem: A regular die is rolled once. Event A: getting a number less than 3; event B: getting a prime number. Then $P(A \cup B)$ equals …
solution: $A \cup B = \{1, 2, 3, 5\}$, so $n(A \cup B) = 4$ and $P(A \cup B) = \dfrac{4}{6} = \dfrac{2}{3}$.
Check by the rule: $A \cap B = \{2\}$, so $P(A) + P(B) - P(A \cap B) = \dfrac{2}{6} + \dfrac{3}{6} - \dfrac{1}{6} = \dfrac{4}{6} = \dfrac{2}{3}$ ✓.
questions.source_note: Original question; union on the die by counting and by the rule, p.33

questions.stem: A and B are two mutually exclusive events in the sample space of a random experiment where $P(B) = 0.3$ and $P(A \cup B) = 0.85$. Find $P(A)$.
solution: A and B are mutually exclusive, so $P(A \cap B) = 0$ and $P(A \cup B) = P(A) + P(B)$.
questions.source_note: Original variant of Drill 1-C (P(A ∩ B) = zero case, new numbers), p.34

questions.stem: If $A \subset S$, then the complementary event $A'$ to the event A satisfies …
solution: The complementary event $A'$ contains all the elements of the sample space S that are not in A.
So $A \cup A' = S$ and $A \cap A' = \phi$ — the event and the complementary event are two mutually exclusive events.
It follows that $P(A) + P(A') = P(S) = 1$.
questions.source_note: Original question; complementary event definition box, p.35

questions.stem: A is an event of the sample space of a random experiment and $A'$ is its complementary event. If $P(A) = 0.7$, find $P(A')$.
solution: Substitute: $P(A') = 1 - 0.7$.
questions.source_note: Original question; P(A′) = 1 − P(A) from the table observation, pp.35-36

questions.stem: A box has identical balls numbered from 1 to 9 and one ball is drawn randomly. Event A: getting a number divisible by 3. The probability of the complementary event $A'$ equals …
solution: $A'$ is the event of NOT getting a number divisible by 3: $A' = \{1, 2, 4, 5, 7, 8\}$, $n(A') = 6$, so $P(A') = \dfrac{6}{9} = \dfrac{2}{3}$.
Another solution: $P(A') = 1 - P(A) = 1 - \dfrac{1}{3} = \dfrac{2}{3}$.
questions.source_note: Original variant of the balls 1–7 even/odd Think-and-Discuss (→ balls 1–9, divisible by 3), p.35

questions.stem: A spinner is divided into 10 equal sectors, 3 of them are red. Find the probability that the indicator does NOT stop on a red sector.
solution: The 10 sectors are equal, so $n(S) = 10$; the event R (red) has $n(R) = 3$, so $P(R) = \dfrac{3}{10}$.
Not stopping on red is the complementary event $R'$.
questions.source_note: Original question; complement applied to the spinner setting of p.31 drill, pp.35-36

questions.stem: A is an event of a sample space S and $A'$ is its complementary event. If $P(A') = \dfrac{2}{5}$, then $P(A)$ equals …
questions.source_note: Original question; P(A) = 1 − P(A′), p.36

questions.stem: A is an event of the sample space of a random experiment and $A'$ is its complementary event. If $P(A) = 3\,P(A')$, find $P(A')$.
solution: Substitute: $3\,P(A') + P(A') = 1$, so $4\,P(A') = 1$.
questions.source_note: Original question; solving with P(A) + P(A′) = 1, p.36

questions.stem: The event A and its complementary event $A'$ are always …

choices.text: two mutually exclusive events whose union is the sample space S

solution: By definition $A \cap A' = \phi$, so the event and the complementary event are two mutually exclusive events — they can never occur together.
Also $A \cup A' = S$: one of them must occur, and $P(A) + P(A') = P(S) = 1$.
Their probabilities are equal only in the special case $P(A) = P(A') = \frac{1}{2}$, not always.
questions.source_note: Original question; the event and its complement are mutually exclusive with union S, p.35

questions.stem: A class contains 30 students, 12 of them wear glasses. If a student is selected randomly, find the probability that the selected student does NOT wear glasses.
solution: $n(S) = 30$; let A be the event that the selected student wears glasses, $n(A) = 12$, so $P(A) = \dfrac{12}{30} = \dfrac{2}{5}$.
Not wearing glasses is the complementary event $A'$, with $n(A') = 30 - 12 = 18$.
$P(A') = \dfrac{18}{30} = \dfrac{3}{5} = 0.6$; another solution: $P(A') = 1 - P(A) = 1 - \dfrac{2}{5} = \dfrac{3}{5}$.
questions.source_note: Original variant of Example 1-B (doesn't read Al-Akhbar → doesn't wear glasses, new numbers), p.36

questions.stem: If A and B are two events of a sample space S, then $A - B$ is the event of …

choices.text: the occurrence of A and the non-occurrence of B (the occurrence of A only)
the occurrence of the two events together
the occurrence of at least one of the two events

solution: $A - B$ (read: A difference B) is the event of the occurrence of A and the non-occurrence of B.
That is: the occurrence of the event A only.
The occurrence together is $A \cap B$, and at least one is $A \cup B$.
questions.source_note: Original question; difference between two events definition box, p.37

questions.stem: For any two events A and B of a sample space S: $(A - B) \cup (A \cap B) = $ …
solution: $A - B$ is the part of A outside B, and $A \cap B$ is the part of A inside B.
Together these two parts make up all of A: $(A - B) \cup (A \cap B) = A$.
In the Venn diagram, the set A is split into exactly these two regions.
questions.source_note: Original question; note (A − B) ∪ (A ∩ B) = A, p.37

questions.stem: A class contains 50 students: 22 play football, 18 play basketball and 10 play both games. If a student is selected randomly, find the probability that the student plays football ONLY.
solution: Let A = plays football and B = plays basketball: $n(S) = 50$, $n(A) = 22$, $n(B) = 18$, $n(A \cap B) = 10$.
Playing football only is the difference $A - B$: $n(A - B) = n(A) - n(A \cap B) = 22 - 10 = 12$.
questions.source_note: Original variant of Example 1 + drill (newspapers 40/18/15/8 → games 50/22/18/10), pp.36-37

questions.stem: In the same class of 50 students (22 play football, 18 play basketball, 10 play both), the probability that a randomly selected student plays basketball ONLY equals …
solution: Playing basketball only is the difference $B - A$: the student plays basketball and does not play football.
questions.source_note: Original variant of drill 2 (reads Al-Ahram only → plays basketball only), p.37

questions.stem: In the same class of 50 students (22 play football, 18 play basketball, 10 play both), find the probability that a randomly selected student plays NEITHER of the two games.
solution: Split the class in the Venn diagram: football only $= 22 - 10 = 12$, both $= 10$, basketball only $= 18 - 10 = 8$.
Students playing at least one game: $n(A \cup B) = 12 + 10 + 8 = 30$.
Playing neither game is the complementary event of $A \cup B$: $n = 50 - 30 = 20$.
$P(\text{neither}) = \dfrac{20}{50} = \dfrac{2}{5} = 0.4$.
questions.source_note: Original question; Venn regions + complement of the union, extends p.36 example

questions.stem: In the same class of 50 students (22 play football, 18 play basketball, 10 play both), the probability that a randomly selected student plays EXACTLY ONE of the two games equals …
solution: Exactly one game means: football only OR basketball only — the union $(A - B) \cup (B - A)$ of two mutually exclusive events.
$n(A - B) = 22 - 10 = 12$ and $n(B - A) = 18 - 10 = 8$, so together $12 + 8 = 20$ students.
questions.source_note: Original variant of drill 3 (Al-Akhbar only or Al-Ahram only → exactly one game), p.37

questions.stem: Identical cards numbered from 1 to 10 are mixed well and a card is drawn randomly. Event A: the number is even; event B: the number is divisible by 4. Then $P(A - B)$ equals …
solution: $A - B$ is the event that A occurs and B does not: $A - B = \{2, 6, 10\}$, so $n(A - B) = 3$.
questions.source_note: Original question; difference of events by listing elements, p.37

questions.stem: A and B are two events of a sample space S where $n(S) = 30$, $n(A) = 15$ and $n(A \cap B) = 6$. Find $P(A - B)$.
solution: Since $(A - B) \cup (A \cap B) = A$ and the two parts are mutually exclusive: $n(A - B) = n(A) - n(A \cap B)$.
questions.source_note: Original question; n(A − B) = n(A) − n(A ∩ B) from the note, p.37

visuals.caption: Every probability lives between 0 and 1 — from the impossible event to the certain event, as a fraction or a percentage.
Rolling a die once: the six equally likely outcomes fill up the sample space — n(S) = 6.

Two overlapping events in a Venn diagram: the middle region A ∩ B is where A and B happen together.
Mutually exclusive events never touch: A ∩ B = φ, so P(A ∩ B) = 0 — they cannot happen at the same time.

A ∪ B covers all three regions — at least one of the two events occurs, so count every element once.

visuals.caption: Add P(A) + P(B), then subtract the overlap counted twice: 0.3 + 0.4 − 0.2 = 0.5.

The complement A′ is everything in the sample space S outside A — together they fill S with no overlap.

visuals.caption: P(A) + P(A′) = 1 — the event and its complement always complete the whole circle.
